title: Number and date an ATM's requests

blocks.text: An ATM network is moving its machines to a new acquirer. Each ATM builds its requests with `AtmRequests`, in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/AtmRequests.java`: balance inquiries, cash withdrawals, and the sign-on it sends when it comes into service. The machines stand in several countries, each with its clock set to local time, and they stay in service for years.

The two card requests are written. Finish the four methods marked `TODO`; the comment on each says what it is for. The acquirer's test team will compare what your messages say with what it receives and what it echoes back, from ATMs in different time zones. About 10 lines in total.

cases.says: a balance inquiry, a withdrawal and a sign-on carry their own MTI and fields, a transmission time and consecutive trace numbers, and each packs with iso87ascii
field 7 is the same GMT time for the same instant, whatever zone the ATM's clock is in
after 999999 the trace number starts again at 000001 and is never 000000
the trace number is set at its full six digits, so the message in memory matches what the host echoes
the sign-on takes the next trace number from the same sequence as the card requests

origin.section: 2.5 The STAN Is One Sequence per Link

concepts: Field 7 is the transmission time in GMT, whatever the zone of the server or of the clock.
The fields every message on a link carries are set in one method of a factory with an injected clock and counter, so every message type gets them alike.
The STAN is one counting sequence per link, shared by every message type, from 000001 to 999999 and around again; random and time-of-day STANs collide.
